spatial_claims.claim: C1 and C2 are similar cylinders with h:k = a:b (proportional axes and diameters). Auxiliary cylinder T constructed with same base as C2 (base B2) and height h (same as C1).
Stacking m congruent copies of T along one axis produces a cylinder on base B2 with height mh; stacking n copies of C2 produces a cylinder on base B2 with height nk.
Placing both stacks with lower bases together and axes aligned: if mh > nk, the shorter stack (nk) is a proper part of the taller stack (mh), since both share base B2.
C1 and T have equal height h. C1 has base B1, T has base B2. Application of 12.11 (equal-height cylinders are as their bases) yields C1:T = B1:B2.
U1 and U2 are cylinders sharing bases and heights with similar cones K1 and K2 respectively; since the axis:diameter ratios are preserved, U1 and U2 are similar cylinders.
By 12.10, U1 = 3*K1 and U2 = 3*K2 (each cylinder is triple its inscribed cone with same base and height).

configuration_map: The configuration involves two similar cylinders C1 (base diameter a, height h) and C2 (base diameter b, height k) with h:k = a:b. An auxiliary cylinder T is constructed sharing C2's base (B2) and C1's height (h), serving as an intermediary for ratio comparison. T connects to C2 via the stacking/Archimedean argument (same base, different heights, giving T:C2 = h:k), and to C1 via 12.11 (same height, different bases, giving C1:T = B1:B2). For cones, K1 and K2 are similar cones, and U1, U2 are their corresponding cylinders (same base and height), which inherit similarity. All constructed objects maintain consistent dimensional relationships throughout.
pass_reason: The proof is predominantly a ratio-and-proportion argument with minimal spatial claims. The spatial constructions (auxiliary cylinder T, cylinder stacking, cone-cylinder correspondence) are all standard solid geometry facts used in mutually consistent configurations. There are no angle decompositions, no interior/exterior point claims, no ray-ordering claims, and no betweenness arguments that could produce contradictions. Every spatial claim is compatible with every other.
